cards.html:
The pipeline must push images and deploy services, so it needs AWS permissions. The old way was to create an IAM user, generate an access key, and store it as a GitHub secret. That key never expires, and if it leaks, someone else can use your account until you notice.

The modern way is OpenID Connect (OIDC). GitHub can issue each job a short-lived, signed ID token (a JWT) that says "I am a workflow run of repository X, on branch Y, in environment Z". You tell AWS to trust tokens from GitHub under specific conditions. The job exchanges the token for temporary AWS credentials that expire after about an hour (Figure 12).

cards.s: The trust policy, line by line
cards.html:
Every IAM role has two policies. The trust policy answers "who may assume this role?". We use one template for all our GitHub roles; setup.sh fills in ACCOUNT_ID, GH_OWNER and SUBJECT:

infra/github-trust-policy.json:

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "GitHubActionsOIDC",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": {
        "Federated": "arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT_ID:oidc-provider/token.actions.githubusercontent.com"
      },
      "Action": "sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity",
      "Condition": {
        "StringEquals": {
          "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:aud": "sts.amazonaws.com",
          "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub": "repo:GH_OWNER/credit-api:SUBJECT"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

cards.s: The trust policy, line by line
cards.html:
LineMeaning
7–9Principal: the identity provider you registered in IAM for token.actions.githubusercontent.com. Only tokens signed by GitHub are considered.
10Action: sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity is the STS call that exchanges an OIDC token for credentials.
13Audience (aud): the token must be meant for AWS STS. configure-aws-credentials requests exactly this audience.
14Subject (sub): who exactly is calling. A push to main gives repo:you/credit-api:ref:refs/heads/main; a job that declares environment: production gives repo:you/credit-api:environment:production. Each role accepts exactly one subject; any other repository, fork, branch or environment is rejected.

cards.s: The trust policy, line by line
cards.html:
Watch out: The classic OIDC security hole

Never use a wildcard such as repo:* or leave out the sub condition. Then every GitHub repository in the world could assume your role. Keep sub as narrow as possible; StringLike with repo:you/credit-api:* is the loosest acceptable form.

Most OIDC problems are a mismatch between the sub that GitHub puts into the token and the list in the trust policy. The format depends on how the job was started, and one rule surprises everybody: if the job declares an environment, the environment wins over the branch.

The job…gets sub =
runs on a push to main, no environmentrepo:you/credit-api:ref:refs/heads/main
runs on a push to feature/xrepo:you/credit-api:ref:refs/heads/feature/x
runs for a pull requestrepo:you/credit-api:pull_request
runs for a tag pushrepo:you/credit-api:ref:refs/tags/v1.4.0
declares environment: production, any triggerrepo:you/credit-api:environment:production

A first version of this pipeline (in the previous edition of this book) used one role that trusted three subjects: main, the staging environment and the production environment, with permission to update any ECS service. A senior reviewer found the hole in five minutes:

What if… a feature branch declares environment: staging?

What happens: Someone pushes a branch with a new workflow whose job says environment: staging. GitHub issues a token with sub = …:environment:staging, which the single role trusted. The job gets AWS credentials and, because the role could update every ECS service, it can deploy unreviewed code to production.

Why: Two weaknesses combined: an environment without rules (anyone on any branch may use staging) and a role broader than any single job needs.

What you do: Close both, as the repository now does. (1) In Settings → Environments, give every environment, staging included, a deployment-branch rule: only main. GitHub then refuses to start a job for that environment from any other branch, so no token is ever issued. (2) Split the role: one per stage, each trusting one subject and allowed to touch only its own resources.

RoleTrusts only sub =May do
github-credit-api-build…:ref:refs/heads/mainPush images to the credit-api repository. Nothing in ECS.
github-credit-api-staging…:environment:stagingUpdate the service credit-api-staging; read images; pass the two ECS roles.
github-credit-api-production…:environment:productionSame, for credit-api-production; tag images prod-….

Now the trust policies read like sentences: only code on main can build; only a job that passed the staging rules can touch staging; only a job a reviewer approved can touch production. A pull request gets sub = …:pull_request and matches no role at all. This is defence in depth: if one control is misconfigured, another still holds. The permissions live in infra/permissions-build.json and infra/permissions-deploy.json; the deploy file is a template in which setup.sh replaces ENV:

infra/permissions-deploy.json (excerpt):

{
      "Sid": "EcsUpdateOnlyThisEnvironment",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [
        "ecs:UpdateExpressGatewayService",
        "ecs:DescribeExpressGatewayService",
        "ecs:DescribeServices",
        "ecs:ListServiceDeployments",
        "ecs:DescribeServiceDeployments",
        "ecs:UntagResource"
      ],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:ecs:eu-central-1:ACCOUNT_ID:service/*/credit-api-ENV"
    },

Watch out: Verify the service ARN pattern

The statement above restricts updates to resources matching service/*/credit-api-staging (or -production), the format ECS uses for service ARNs. This edition could not run it against AWS. If the first deployment fails with AccessDenied on UpdateExpressGatewayService, the error names the resource it tried; compare it with the output of aws ecs list-services --cluster default and adjust the pattern. In a company, the stronger version of this idea is one AWS account per environment (Chapter 9).

What if… the AWS login step fails with "Not authorized to perform sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity"?

What happens: configure-aws-credentials fails with Could not assume role with OIDC: Not authorized to perform sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity.

Why: AWS rejected the token. AWS does not tell you which condition failed (that would help attackers), so check in this order:

  1. Which sub did this job get? Use the table above. Typical: you added environment: staging to a job, and its sub changed from ref:refs/heads/main to environment:staging, which is not in the policy. Or the workflow runs on a PR.
  2. Typos. The owner in repo:You/credit-api must match GitHub's spelling; the repository name too. StringEquals compares exactly.
  3. Audience. aud must be sts.amazonaws.com.
  4. Provider. The OIDC provider exists in this account, and the role's Principal contains this account ID.
  5. Role ARN. vars.AWS_ROLE_ARN is an environment variable: in a job without that environment it is empty or points elsewhere.

What you do: Fix the workflow, or the subject in setup.sh and run it again: it updates existing trust policies (aws iam update-assume-role-policy). AWS CloudTrail records each failed AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity call, which can confirm that it was tried and by which role.

What if… the error is "Credentials could not be loaded" instead?

What happens: Credentials could not be loaded, please check your action inputs: Could not load credentials from any providers.

Why: The job never got an OIDC token at all, so AWS was not even asked: permissions: id-token: write is missing. A common way to lose it: you add a permissions: block to a job (for example contents: write to create a release). Job-level permissions replace the workflow-level ones; they are not merged.

What you do: List everything the job needs in its own block: permissions: {id-token: write, contents: read}. In a reusable workflow, the caller must grant it as well.

What if… the login works, but docker push says "not authorized"?

What happens: denied: User: arn:aws:sts::…:assumed-role/github-actions-… is not authorized to perform: ecr:InitiateLayerUpload.

Why: Authentication succeeded (you are the role); authorisation failed: the permissions policy does not allow this action on this resource. Different ECR repository name, different region in the ARN, or a missing action.

What you do: The message names the exact action and role. Add the action for the exact resource ARN to the permissions policy; resist the temptation of ecr:* on *. Least privilege means you will see this error a few times while building a pipeline, and each time the message tells you precisely what is missing.

infra/setup.sh creates the ECR repository, the OIDC provider, the three GitHub roles and the two roles ECS Express Mode needs. Every step first checks whether its resource exists, so you can run it again after changing a policy (an idempotent script, the property that infrastructure-as-code tools give you for free, Chapter 8). Read it before running it, then:

terminal:

aws sso login
GH_OWNER=<your-github-user> bash infra/setup.sh

Afterwards add the variables below in GitHub. None of them is secret: an ARN is an address, not a password. Most are repository variables (Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → Variables); AWS_ROLE_ARN is an environment variable, set once in each environment (Settings → Environments → staging → Add variable), so the same workflow line resolves to a different role per environment.

VariableValue
AWS_BUILD_ROLE_ARNarn:aws:iam::<account>:role/github-credit-api-build
AWS_ROLE_ARN (staging)…:role/github-credit-api-staging
AWS_ROLE_ARN (production)…:role/github-credit-api-production
ECS_EXECUTION_ROLE_ARNarn:aws:iam::<account>:role/ecsTaskExecutionRole
ECS_INFRA_ROLE_ARN…:role/ecsInfrastructureRoleForExpressServices
ECR_REGISTRY<account>.dkr.ecr.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com

OptionGood atWhy not here
ECS Express Mode (Fargate)One API call creates service, load balancer, HTTPS URL, autoscaling and canary deployments. You still see and own every resource.Our choice.
ECS on Fargate, hand-builtFull control over VPC, load balancer, task definitions.Twenty resources to wire up before the first request; that belongs in an IaC lesson (Level 5).
AWS LambdaPay per request, scales to zero.Cold starts with a 500 MB ML image; 15-minute limit. Shown as an optional variant.

AWS App RunnerWas the simplest "container → URL" service.Closed to new customers since April 2026 (box below).

Concept: AWS App Runner: what you should know

App Runner (2021) took a container image or a source repository and gave you an HTTPS URL with automatic scaling, without load balancers or clusters. You paid per vCPU and GB while instances were active. On 30 April 2026 AWS closed App Runner to new customers (per AWS's availability notice when this edition was written; verify). Existing customers can still use it and create services, and AWS keeps patching it, but no new features are planned. AWS recommends ECS Express Mode as the replacement, and publishes a migration guide that shifts traffic with weighted DNS (a blue-green technique, Level 5). In interviews: you may meet App Runner in existing stacks; for new work you would choose ECS Express Mode or ECS on Fargate.

Amazon ECS (Elastic Container Service) runs containers. A task is a running container (or a group of them). A service keeps N copies of a task running and replaces failed ones. Fargate runs tasks without you managing servers. An Application Load Balancer (ALB) receives HTTPS traffic and forwards it to healthy tasks; it uses our /health endpoint to decide which tasks are healthy. Express Mode creates all of this in your account's default VPC (network) and gives each service a URL like https://<name>.ecs.eu-central-1.on.aws.

Watch out: What it costs

Approximate Frankfurt prices (November 2026; check the AWS Pricing Calculator): one ALB ≈ 0.03 USD/hour; each Fargate task with 0.25 vCPU and 0.5 GB ≈ 0.015 USD/hour; public IPv4 addresses 0.005 USD/hour each. Staging plus production together: roughly 2 USD per day, about 60 USD per month if forgotten. Your budget alarms will warn you, but the habit to build is: clean up after each session (Section 5.6).
